Degeneracy and caveats: The standard terminal oxidase. Its presence alone does not indicate a microaerobic lifestyle.
Strong signal of a microaerobic niche. Expected in circumneutral FeOB, Aquificota and Campylobacterota, which cannot tolerate full aeration.
The other high-affinity oxidase; often present alongside cbb3. Also functions in oxidative stress defence, so presence alone is not proof of a microaerobic lifestyle.

In monooxygenase systems O2 is incorporated into the substrate, so it is a substrate before it is a terminal acceptor. When these are present, the regime is aerobic even if the paper states no acceptor.
Most important degeneracy: shares K00370/K00371 with nxrAB (nitrite oxidation, the reverse reaction). Resolve by localisation signal (Tat), subunit composition and phylogenetic placement.
Periplasmic nitrate reductase; not degenerate with nxrAB, so its presence is cleaner evidence for the reductive direction.
The committed step of denitrification. The two types are functionally equivalent and mutually exclusive in most genomes, so screen for both.
Reduces NO to N2O. Absence with nirK/nirS present implies NO toxicity and is worth checking.

Presence means denitrification runs to N2; absence means it stops at N2O. Strains with the same donor-acceptor pair differ in this gene, so never borrow it from another strain of the same species. N2O is a potent greenhouse gas, making this an ecologically important trait.
Dissimilatory reduction of nitrite to ammonium, a branch point competing with denitrification. nrfA presence with nosZ absence distinguishes DNRA from truncated denitrification.
Diagnostic for anammox and found nowhere else. NH4+ is the donor, making this the one set where both partners are nitrogen species.
Oxidises hydrazine to N2. Related to hao (K10535) in sequence, so check the taxonomy (Planctomycetota) as well.
Activates sulfate to APS. Shared with sulfur oxidisers running the pathway in reverse (directional degeneracy).
Shared with sulfur oxidisers. The partner complex distinguishes direction: QmoABC in reducers, AprM in oxidisers.

Most important degeneracy: identical KOs to the reverse-acting rDsr of sulfur oxidisers. Resolve by (1) placement in a dsrAB reference tree, (2) absence of dsrEFH (retained only in the oxidative direction), (3) QmoABC vs AprM. Note that an explicit statement of obligate anaeroby in the literature settles the direction without sequence work.
Couples DsrAB to the membrane. Its presence supports a genuinely respiratory (dissimilatory) pathway rather than assimilatory sulfate reduction.
Present in the reductive direction; the oxidative direction uses AprM instead. One of the three criteria for calling dsrAB direction.
A route to sulfide independent of DsrAB, found in some organisms that reduce sulfite but not sulfate.

KO: Closely related to psrABC (K08352); poor KO resolution
Degeneracy and caveats: Most sulfate reducers use thiosulfate as a secondary acceptor. Hard to separate from polysulfide reductase by KO alone. Remember that the same compound is a donor in aerobic sulfur oxidisers.
Reduces S0 to HS-. Sequences are highly similar to hydrogenases and to polysulfide reductase, so annotation mix-ups are common.
Because S0 is insoluble, many organisms in fact reduce polysulfide (Sn 2-) generated in solution. Cultivation notes about colloidal versus powdered sulfur bear on this.
Several sulfur reductases are hydrogenase homologues. Without functional evidence, a hydrogenase hit may actually be a sulfur reductase.
The Shewanella-type extracellular electron transfer conduit. Not detectable through KEGG.
The Geobacter-type multiheme cytochrome network. Mechanisms differ widely between organisms, so a single marker set does not cover all iron reducers.

Proposed for anaerobic Fe(III) reduction in acidophilic Acidithiobacillus, but unsettled. Such strains use the same couple in both directions, so a genome alone cannot call the direction; the phenotype (does it oxidise Fe(II)?) decides.
The decisive marker for methanogenesis, found nowhere else. Also present in anaerobic methane oxidisers (ANME) running in reverse, so check the taxonomy when the context allows it.
The entry step that fixes CO2 onto methanofuran. Confirms the hydrogenotrophic route rather than the acetoclastic one.
Generates the sodium-motive force. Its absence points to a methylotrophic methanogen rather than the hydrogenotrophic route.
Forms the electron-bifurcating Mvh-Hdr complex, the precondition for this set given its small delta-E.

The core of the WL pathway. CO2 here is both terminal acceptor and carbon source. Its presence alongside aerobic sulfur oxidation markers is contradictory (CODH/ACS is oxygen sensitive) and should prompt suspicion of a misannotation.
Forms the bifunctional CODH/ACS complex with acsB. Also serves as the CO donor marker, so the same gene appears on the donor sheet.
At 124 mV this set has the smallest delta-E in the matrix, so either Rnf or Ech is mandatory. Which one is present separates the two energetic types of acetogen.
The alternative to Rnf. Moorella-type acetogens use Ech, Acetobacterium-type use Rnf.
The final steps producing acetate and substrate-level ATP. Confirms that the product is acetate rather than another WL end product.

Functional group: Scope: the eight major acceptor groups (O2, nitrate/denitrification, anammox, sulfate, sulfur, iron, CO2 for methanogenesis, CO2 for acetogenesis). Minor acceptors (Mn(IV), As(V), SeO4 2-, ClO3-, fumarate, DMSO/TMAO) are omitted here; see Electron_Acceptors.

Priority: Essential = indispensable for calling the physiotype; Alternative = a different route to the same function; Supporting = for confirming the route or downstream steps. Rows marked Difficult or No need a custom HMM or a dedicated tool.

Note the asymmetry with the donor sheet: S, N and Fe appear on both sides, and S0 and NO2- occur as donor and acceptor alike. Direction must be called from the oxygen regime, the wording of the description, or phylogenetic placement, not from the KO.
In methanogens and acetogens CO2 serves as both terminal acceptor and carbon source, so these rows also overlap with CO2_Fixation_Pathways (WL).
